research:
Today's Essex accent is largely Cockney that moved out with the post-war families rehoused in Debden, Basildon, Harlow and similar estates and New Towns. Linguists call it the Cockney diaspora, and Essex is now where most traditional Cockney features are heard (QMUL / Sue Fox: https://www.qmul.ac.uk/news/latest-news/2013/hss/present-day-cockney-speakers-more-likely-to-live-in-essex-than-the-east-end-of-london.html).
Amanda Cole's Debden studies found that the first Essex-raised generation kept almost every Cockney feature, and that Essex-born men call their own accent 'Essex' rather than Cockney. Older London-born speakers are broader. Younger and Essex-born speakers are milder, with fewer dropped h's and less extreme vowels (https://theconversation.com/the-cockney-dialect-is-not-dead-its-just-called-essex-now-196447 ; https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/dialect-2022-0005/html ; https://repository.essex.ac.uk/29772/).
Estuary English is the milder middle of a continuum running from RP to Cockney along the Thames. It is closer to RP in grammar but shares some Cockney sounds. A man of about 50 from south Essex sits between Estuary and broad Essex (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estuary_English).
It differs from South London speech in where it comes from: it is East End Cockney carried east and levelled out in the suburbs, not the Multicultural London English that has replaced Cockney in inner London (Cole and Evans 2020, Language in Society: https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/journals/language-in-society/article/abs/phonetic-variation-and-change-in-the-cockney-diaspora-the-role-of-place-gender-and-identity/68653062DDBD66EEE307A87CBC0B3FD3).
The stigma that used to attach to Cockney now attaches to Essex, especially the south. The caricature is the TV and reality-show version: every feature pushed at once, bright and showy. A real man of 50 is plain and level and only moderately broad, so the designs name a real town, an ordinary background and a low voice, and leave the accent mild.

designs.name: jim-r2-a
designs.desc: A man of about fifty from Basildon, Essex, with a mild Essex accent. He has an ordinary low, slightly rough voice and speaks plainly at an easy conversational pace.
designs.why: Basildon is the textbook New Town Essex accent, and naming the town plus 'mild' should give the real thing without any acting.

designs.name: jim-r2-b
designs.desc: A man in his late fifties who grew up on the council estate in Debden, Essex, with East End parents, and has a light Essex accent. His voice is deep and a little gravelly, and he speaks plainly and without hurry.
designs.why: Debden is the best-documented case of the diaspora, so it should be the most authentically broad, with the gravel and age keeping it grounded.

designs.name: jim-r2-e
designs.desc: A man of about fifty-two from Grays in Thurrock, Essex, who has worked around the Tilbury docks all his life and has a subtle Essex accent. His voice is low and flat, and he speaks quietly and plainly.
designs.why: The Thames-side working background is a real estuary man, and the flat, quiet voice suits banter that isn't a big sell.

designs.name: jim-r2-d
designs.desc: A man of about fifty-five from Harlow, Essex, a builder by trade, with a subtle Essex accent. His voice is low and slightly hoarse from years of outdoor work, and he speaks plainly.
designs.why: A Harlow tradesman is a believable car-boot regular, though 'hoarse' could tip into a rasp the engine overdoes.

designs.name: jim-r2-c
designs.desc: A man of about forty-eight from Southend-on-Sea, Essex, with a light Estuary accent. He has a medium-low, slightly husky voice and speaks plainly in an everyday way.
designs.why: This is the subtlest option and a safe fallback, but Southend plus 'Estuary' risks drifting toward neutral or posh.
